analysis.one_liner: Requires FDA premarket approval and public safety review for genetically engineered foods.
analysis.headline: The bill never advanced past a Senate committee: it was introduced in October 2000 with no cosponsors, referred to the Agriculture Committee, and died when the Congress ended in January 2001.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required companies to get government approval before selling a genetically engineered food, instead of the voluntary process that existed at the time. Companies would have had to submit their safety research to the FDA, and that research would have been made public. It also would have created government testing of foods in the marketplace, a public registry of engineered foods, and federal research grants on the economic and environmental risks of food biotechnology.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers, who would gain a mandatory safety review before any new genetically engineered food reaches grocery shelves, and whose confidence in the food supply the bill aimed to protect by making safety data public [S2][S3]. Allergic consumers in particular would benefit from the bill's priority on research to detect potential allergens in engineered plants [S3]. Small farms would also gain a research program examining biotechnology's impact on the farm economy [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Would replace the FDA's voluntary consultation process with mandatory premarket approval, so no genetically engineered food could legally enter commerce without an FDA safety finding [S2][S3].
Would require companies to submit all research and test results to the FDA and make those materials publicly available, including on the Internet, before any approval decision [S2][S3].
Would let any person request an additional FDA review of a previously approved food when new scientific evidence emerges, and let the FDA withdraw approval if a food is found unsafe [S3].
Would create a marketplace testing program to detect unapproved or restricted engineered ingredients from the farm to the retail store, including in imported foods [S2][S3].
Would establish a public registry identifying every engineered food submitted for approval, its regulatory status, and the genetic changes made to it [S3].
Would fund competitive research grants on the economic and environmental risks and benefits of biotechnology in food production, with priority on better tests for potential allergens [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Producers of genetically engineered foods — the seed and agricultural biotechnology companies that develop these crops, plus food companies that import or use engineered ingredients — would bear the cost of mandatory premarket approval, testing, and public disclosure of safety research, along with approval delays [S2][S3]. Taxpayers would fund the new testing program, registry, and research grants [S3].

drawbacks.text: Mandatory premarket approval would add regulatory costs and delays for companies developing engineered crops, potentially slowing products that could benefit farmers and consumers; the bill's own findings acknowledge the 'enormous' potential positive effects of these foods while imposing a review gate on all of them [S3].

The bill builds on the FDA's existing 1992 policy and 1997 voluntary consultation process rather than replacing the science behind it, so its practical addition is largely making the process mandatory and public; critics could argue the existing process already covered safety assessment [S3].
The bill does not require labeling of genetically engineered foods; it only requires agencies to report on labeling options, leaving the consumer-transparency question it raised unresolved [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's core value is transparency and a mandatory safety gate: companies would no longer decide privately with the FDA whether an engineered food is safe, and the public could see the data. The costs are real but standard for food-safety regulation — industry compliance costs, slower product approvals, and taxpayer-funded testing and research. The bill is a measured version of oversight: it includes exemptions for well-reviewed food categories and foods regulated under other law, and it keeps existing trade-secret protections. Its main weakness is that it stops short of labeling, the transparency measure most consumers associate with this debate.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Agriculture Committee, which never took it up, and it died when the Congress ended three months later.

narrative.text: Sen. Durbin introduced the Genetically Engineered Foods Act in the Senate on October 11, 2000 [S1][S5].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry; no further action was taken on it [S5].
The 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001, and bills not passed by then expire [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The agricultural biotechnology industry is better off because the bill died: it avoided mandatory premarket FDA approval, public disclosure of safety research, and marketplace testing of engineered foods. Consumers did not get the mandatory safety review the bill would have provided.

for.name: Sen. Richard Durbin
for.role: U.S. Senator from Illinois; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks; no senator joined as a cosponsor

against.name: Senate Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Never acted on the bill after referral; no markup, no vote, no report before the Congress ended

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever held and no opposition is recorded in the action history, so the partisan shape cannot be determined; the bill's single sponsor was a Democrat and it drew no cosponsors of either party [S4][S5].

industries.note: The bill would have forced these companies to obtain FDA approval before marketing any engineered food and to make their safety research public, replacing the voluntary consultation process under which they operated. Public confidence in engineered foods was the stated reason, and companies would have borne the compliance costs and disclosure of proprietary data [S2][S3].

industries.industry: Food manufacturers and importers using engineered ingredients
industries.note: They would face liability under the bill's prohibited-acts provisions for selling foods that never went through approval, and importers would face the same rules as domestic producers. But the bill also promised to maintain consumer confidence in the food supply, which the industry had an interest in preserving [S2][S3].
A new competitive grant program would fund research on biotechnology's economic and environmental effects, with priority on allergen-detection methods [S3].
